prime.problem: KMP answers "where does this one pattern occur". Many string questions instead ask "are these two substrings equal?" thousands of times, for example to find any repeated substring. Comparing characters costs O(L) each time; you want an O(1) fingerprint per window.
prime.fits: Second Strings card, supplemented beside KMP. It reuses binary search on the answer ("a repeat of length L exists" is monotone) and hash sets from cs-1, and it is the interview alternative to the suffix automaton that follows.
prime.goal: Compute and slide a rolling hash by hand, estimate its collision risk for a given n and p, and use it with binary search for Longest Duplicate Substring.

attend: In the slide formula, why do you subtract t_i · B^(m−1) before multiplying by B?
Why must the base be at least the alphabet size?
Why does Rabin–Karp still compare characters on a hash hit, and what does a spurious hit cost?
Why is one modulus of about 10⁹ fine for one pattern but not for a set of 10⁵ windows?
Why is "a repeat of length L exists" monotone in L, so you can binary search it?

must: Read a window as an m-digit number in base B mod p → sliding right = remove the leaving digit's weight B^(m−1), shift by B, add the entering digit → each window's hash in O(1) → substring equality becomes integer equality

Different strings can share a hash (172 of the 17,576 three-letter strings share 30 mod 101) → a hash hit is only a candidate → verify characters on every hit → correctness is kept, and spurious hits only cost time

One pattern vs n windows: ≈ n/p false hits; a set of n windows vs itself: ≈ C(n, 2)/p colliding pairs (≈ 5 for n = 10⁵, p ≈ 10⁹) → the birthday effect → double hash (p₁p₂ ≈ 10¹⁸) or verify, with a random base against adversaries
A length-L repeat implies a length-(L − 1) repeat → monotone → binary search L with an O(n) hash-set pass per test → Longest Duplicate Substring in O(n log n) expected ("banana" → "ana" in two tests)
elevated: Python's % returns a value in 0 … p − 1 even for negatives → the slide's negative intermediate needs no fix-up; in C or Java add p first
reference: the exact hashes for abracadabra's windows
the (m − 1)/p proven collision bound for a random base

compress.prompt: From memory, write the slide formula with each term labelled, then two lines: when a hash hit must be verified and why, and how the birthday problem changes the modulus you need.
checklist: h = Σ t · B^(m−1−k) mod p; slide in O(1)
B ≥ alphabet size; p a large prime
equal hashes are candidates; check characters to confirm
one pattern: false hits ≈ n/p; all-pairs set: ≈ n²/(2p)
double hash or random base against collisions and adversaries
binary search L + hash set of windows → longest repeat

retrieve.q: Explain why a rolling hash turns "find a repeated substring of length L" into an O(n) pass, when comparing substrings directly would be O(nL) or worse.
answer: each window's hash comes from the previous one in O(1)
a set of hashes detects a repeat with one lookup per window
only hash hits need an O(L) character check, and those are rare for large p

retrieve.q: Walk through the slide from h("aca") = 41 to h("cad") with B = 256, p = 101 and B² mod p = 88.
answer: take mod 101: 11, matching the card's window table

retrieve.q: Longest Duplicate Substring in an interview: rolling hash + binary search, or a suffix automaton? Compare time, code size and risk.
answer: hash + binary search: O(n log n) expected, under 20 lines, needs collision handling (double hash or verify)
suffix automaton: O(n) deterministic, but clone logic is easy to get wrong under time pressure
the hash version is usually what the interviewer expects; the automaton wins for streaming input or many substring queries

compare.q: KMP never has false positives and rolling hash can. Why would you ever choose the hash, and for which question can KMP not substitute at all?
answer: the hash gives any window's fingerprint in O(1), so it can fill a set of windows or compare arbitrary substring pairs
KMP only finds occurrences of one fixed pattern
for repeat detection, many same-length patterns or 2-D grids, the hash is the tool; for one pattern with a guarantee, KMP

compare.q: A Python set hashes the whole string each time; this card hashes windows incrementally. What does each cost per window of length L, and what collision risk does each leave you with?
answer: set of substrings: O(L) to build each key and hash it, plus O(L) memory per stored substring
rolling hash: O(1) per window, and you store integers
the set compares full strings on collision, so it's exact; the rolling hash needs explicit verification or a double hash

predict.q: Run the binary search for Longest Duplicate Substring on mississippi (lo 1, hi 10). Predict how many length tests it takes and the answer.
predict.answer: Four tests: L = 5 (no repeat → hi = 4), L = 2 ("is" repeats → lo = 3), L = 3 ("iss" → lo = 4), L = 4 ("issi" → lo = 5), then lo > hi. Answer "issi", matching the suffix automaton card. Note "issi" overlaps itself (positions 1 and 4): hashing windows handles overlaps with no special case.

apply.task: With B = 256 and p = 101, compute h("ada") from h("cad") = 11 by one slide, then h("dab") from it. Check both against the card's window table. Then estimate the colliding pairs for a set of 10⁵ windows with p = 10⁹ + 7, and with a second modulus 10⁹ + 9 added.
apply.done: Slides give 95 and 97, matching the table; collisions ≈ 4,999,950,000 / (10⁹ + 7) ≈ 5.0 with one modulus and ≈ 5.0 × 10⁻⁹ with two.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: the number of length tests, or the overlapping answer?
Could you explain why hash hits must be verified, and why that never costs correctness?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: slide formula → O(1) per window, or number of windows → collision risk?
Would you trust a single 10⁹ modulus for a 10⁵-window set? What would you tell an interviewer?
What will you look for in Manacher: a string algorithm that reuses earlier work without any hashing?
